title: The Blue Dogs Were Once Majority Makers—This Cycle They Haven't Barked
author: Julian Andreone
content:

media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F929e3572-c9e5-4599-9e87-ac86cb8cd87d_6466x4312.jpeg)Blue
Dog Reps. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, D-Wash., and Mike Thompson, D-Calif., leave
the U.S. Capitol on November 9, 2023. Photo by Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc
via Getty Images.

The last time that a blue wave powered Democrats to a House majority in 2018,
11 so-called Blue Dogs ousted Republicans, leaving the party in charge with a
slim majority. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi would affectionately refer to the
Blue Dogs as "majority makers," explaining that their conservative politics
may be out of step with the party's base, but without them, the party would be
nowhere.

The same was true in 2006 and 2008, when Blue Dogs made the difference for
Democrats, exactly as they had promised to do when they organized themselves
in 1995 in response to the 1994 Republican wave.

This cycle, instead of taking on Republican incumbents and working to maximize
a potential Democratic majority, the Blue Dogs have been spending their scarce
resources against other Democrats. A review of financial disclosures, coupled
with interviews of campaign operatives, reveal that the coalition's largest
expenditure since the primaries has boosted Mike Thompson, [treasurer of the
Blue Dog PAC](https://www.dropsitenews.com/p/california-election-mike-
thompson-blue-dog-pac), against another Democrat.

This decision is all the more confusing considering that the Blue Dogs backed
a candidate in Florida during the primary who is facing an uphill battle
against Republican Ryan Elijah. Blue Dog Action spent $700,000 during the
primary to get Bale Dalton over the top in Florida's 7th district, beating out
two Democrats to his left. Cook Political Report shifted the race from Likely
R to Lean R in the days before the election.

Instead of putting more money behind Dalton, the super PAC has dumped $1.73
million into a general election in California that pits Thompson against
another Democrat, Eric Jones, a venture capitalist who has spent $15 million
self-funding his anti-corporate, populist campaign focused on getting
corporate money out of politics. In other words, rather than spend money
helping Democrats retake the majority, Blue Dog Action is spending to maintain
their dwindling position.

Blue Dog Action Fund is also dedicating the closing days of the election to
complaining about another Democrat running, Matt Dunlap. Last year, Dunlap
launched a primary challenge to Rep. Jared Golden, a former co-chair of the
Blue Dog Coalition. Golden responded by retiring, and the Democratic
Congressional Campaign Committee got behind State Sen. Joe Baldacci in the
primary, arguing that Dunlap was too progressive to win the general election.
Dunlap won the primary narrowly, the party rallied behind him, and now he
faces Republican Paul LePage.

But the Blue Dogs haven't forgiven Dunlap. The co-founder of the Blue Dog's
super PAC recently went on the record criticizing the House Majority PAC's
decision to invest in Maine instead of Florida's 7th district. "I'm not sure
what HMP was thinking here," said Phil Gardner, referring to House Majority
PAC's decision to cut ad reservations in FL-07 from $3.9 million to $1.95
million, calling it "bonkers they're dumping so much money" behind Dunlap in
favor of Dalton--who he called "one of the party's best recruits."

Gardner, who was speaking to
[Axios](https://www.axios.com/2026/10/20/2026-election-democrats-spending-
districts-cash), is a senior advisor to Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez
(D-Wash.).

Republicans, meanwhile, have spent more than $11 million to date supporting
former Governor Paul LePage there, signaling that the GOP believes the race is
extremely competitive.

HMP recommitted an additional $1.7 million investment in Florida roughly one
week after Gardner's critiques were published. Defending this decision,
Gardner told Drop Site that, "Spending for Red to Blue candidates in tied
races is the entire reason HMP exists. I can't believe any 'Democratic
campaign operative' thinks it's the job of a group besides HMP to do HMP's
core mission."

With their spending decisions this cycle, critical Democratic colleagues say,
the Blue Dogs are forfeiting the argument that while they may be out of step
politically with the base of the party on issues like Medicare for All, at
least they are important to win a majority.

"Money has to be moved to the races that are in most need, regardless of what
flavor of Democrat they are," a Democratic member of Congress granted
anonymity to weigh in, said. "Any group that is advocating for a certain type
of Democrat should use their money where it matters first and not dictate to
those trying to get a majority as a priority."

A national Democratic operative concurred. "Instead of spending the final days
of the midterms working to grow their caucus and help take back the House--
they're attacking red-to-blue candidates and wasting close to $2 million on a
Safe D race," the operative said. "It's one of the most idiotic things I've
ever seen."

Gardner dismissed criticisms of Blue Dog Action's spending choices, saying,
"Given that I've discussed both of those investments in advance with HMP's
leadership, I can't imagine HMP is anything but grateful for BDA PAC's support
of Adam Gray, a Frontline incumbent, and Mike Thompson, an ally of Leader
Jeffries, given HMP's priorities elsewhere on the electoral map."

The Blue Dogs are also spending $425,000 to protect incumbent Rep. Adam Gray.
In this race, there's a Republican on the other side, though [Cook Political
Report lists the California district as "likely
Dem."](https://www.cookpolitical.com/house/race/481881)

Blue Dog PAC, a distinct entity from Blue Dog Action, has contributed directly
to Democrats running for seats currently held by Republicans at other times
this cycle,
[including](https://www.fec.gov/data/disbursements/?data_type=processed&committee_id=C00305318&recipient_name=C00926949&two_year_transaction_period=2026)
$5,000 to Dalton. Other recipients
[received](https://www.fec.gov/data/disbursements/?data_type=processed&committee_id=C00305318&recipient_name=C00844993&recipient_name=C00914119&recipient_name=C00919985&two_year_transaction_period=2026)
$10,000, including Rebecca Cooke, taking on Rep. Derrick Van Orden in WI-03,
Jamie Ager, running for the NC-11 seat currently held by Rep. Chuck Edwards,
and Bobby Pulido, challenging Rep. Monica De La Cruz in TX-15. And Johnny
Garcia, running in TX-35 after Texas Republicans redrew it, has [taken
home](https://www.fec.gov/data/disbursements/?data_type=processed&committee_id=C00305318&recipient_name=C00922799&two_year_transaction_period=2026)
the biggest slice of the pie among Blue Dog challengers at $12,500 in his
contest against Carlos De La Cruz, the brother of the aforementioned
congresswoman.

Blue Dog PAC raised a total of $2,196,255 this cycle, and has spent roughly
$20,000 more than that. Blue Dog Action, on the other hand, has raised
$7,267,677 and spent $6,852,972. As it stands, the Blue Dog Coalition only has
10 members remaining in Congress--Gluesenkamp Perez, Golden, Thompson and
Gray, as well as Reps. Vicente Gonzalez, Luis Correa, Sanford Bishop, Jim
Costa, Henry Cuellar, and Josh Gottheimer. Three of the ten are in competitive
races, and Golden, of course, is leaving Congress.

"BDA PAC sent $225,000 to HMP within the last two weeks for HMP to support
their general election activities, and I have encouraged BDA PAC's donors to
give to HMP for general election spending on Blue Dog candidates. So I'm
confident on the whole this cycle Blue Dog Action has more than done its part
to support House Democrats in their work to win the majority," Gardner said.
